pos: n. (a chief man of the house of Tola, of the tribe of Issachar)
etymology: Hebrew Yizrachyah, the LORD will shine forth, or whom Jehovah brings to light, from zarach, to rise or shine, with Yah; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:3.
biblical_def: Izrahiah appears in the muster of Issachar: “And the sons of Uzzi; Izrahiah: and the sons of Izrahiah; Michael, and Obadiah, and Joel, Ishiah, five: all of them chief men” (1 Chronicles 7:3). The tribe is being counted as a fighting force. Of Tola it is said that his sons “were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred” (1 Chronicles 7:2), and of the whole kindred, “their brethren among all the families of Issachar were valiant men of might, reckoned in all by their genealogies fourscore and seven thousand” (1 Chronicles 7:5). Izrahiah is one head of a father's house in that reckoning, with four sons who were likewise chief men. Issachar is the tribe of whom it was later said that they “were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do” (1 Chronicles 12:32). The name means the LORD shines forth, and the men of this house are recorded as those who could see by that light what the hour required.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Izrahiah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the LORD will shine forth; a chief man of the house of Tola in Issachar, 1 Chronicles 7:3.
webster_full: Hebrew Yizrachyah, the LORD will shine forth, or whom Jehovah brings to light.
From zarach, to rise as the sun, to shine or break forth, with Yah.
It occurs once in the Authorized Version, 1 Chronicles 7:3.
He is reckoned a son of Uzzi, of the house of Tola, in Issachar.
His four sons are named with him, all of them chief men.
scriptures: And the sons of Uzzi; Izrahiah: and the sons of Izrahiah; Michael, and Obadiah, and Joel, Ishiah, five: all of them chief men.

And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father's house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred.
And their brethren among all the families of Issachar were valiant men of might, reckoned in all by their genealogies fourscore and seven thousand.

And of the children of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do; the heads of them were two hundred; and all their brethren were at their commandment.
corruption_summary: Discernment is reduced to opinion-taking; Issachar's chief men had understanding of the times because they first had a covenant to read them by.
corruption_paragraphs: To have understanding of the times is now taken to mean fluency in current affairs — reading the mood and following it. That is not what is said of Issachar. They knew what Israel ought to do, which is a moral judgment, and it rested on knowing what God had already commanded Israel to be. Without the second, the first is only sentiment with a long memory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reading the age rightly requires a fixed standard outside the age. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isaiah 8:20). Izrahiah's name says the LORD shines forth; the men of his house judged the hour by that light and not by the hour itself.

pos: n. (a son of Simeon; also a chief man summoned by Ezra; also a priest who had taken a strange wife)
etymology: Hebrew Yariv, he will contend, or he striveth, from riv, to strive, contend or plead a cause; named at 1 Chronicles 4:24, Ezra 8:16 and Ezra 10:18.
biblical_def: Three men bear this name, and all three stand near a controversy, which the name itself anticipates. The first is a son of Simeon: “The sons of Simeon were, Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul” (1 Chronicles 4:24). The second is one of the chief men Ezra summoned at the river Ahava when he found no Levites in the company: “Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib” (Ezra 8:16), men of understanding sent to Iddo to fetch ministers for the house of God. The third is a priest named in the painful list at the end of the book: “And among the sons of the priests there were found that had taken strange wives: namely, of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren; Maaseiah, and Eliezer, and Jarib, and Gedaliah” (Ezra 10:18). What follows is not excused: “And they gave their hands that they would put away their wives; and being guilty, they offered a ram of the flock for their trespass” (Ezra 10:19). A name meaning he will contend sits over a priest who had to contend first with himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Jarib, a Hebrew proper name signifying he will contend; borne by a son of Simeon, by a chief man under Ezra, and by a priest who had taken a strange wife.
webster_full: Hebrew Yariv, he will contend, or he pleadeth.
From riv, to strive, to contend, or to plead a cause at law.
It occurs three times in the Authorized Version: 1 Chronicles 4:24, Ezra 8:16, Ezra 10:18.
The first is reckoned among the sons of Simeon.
The last is a priest of the sons of Jeshua who put away a strange wife.
scriptures: The sons of Simeon were, Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul:
Ezr 8:16

Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding.
And among the sons of the priests there were found that had taken strange wives: namely, of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren; Maaseiah, and Eliezer, and Jarib, and Gedaliah.
And they gave their hands that they would put away their wives; and being guilty, they offered a ram of the flock for their trespass.
corruption_summary: Repentance is redefined as an inward posture with no cost attached; Ezra 10 records hands given, wives put away, and a trespass offering brought.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern penitence often stops at acknowledgement. The sin is named, feelings are expressed, and nothing is undone. Ezra 10 will not have it. The priests who had married outside the covenant gave their hands — a formal pledge — put away the wives, and brought a ram for their trespass. The text calls them guilty while they are doing it, because doing right afterward does not unmake the wrong.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true repentance is restitution-shaped. “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of” (2 Corinthians 7:10). The priests of Jarib's company did the hardest thing the law required of them, and the Holy Ghost recorded their names doing it, which is itself a mercy toward them.

pos: n. (the captain of the ward who arrested Jeremiah in the gate of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Yir'iyyah, the LORD seeth, or whom Jehovah looks upon, from ra'ah, to see, with Yah; named twice, Jeremiah 37:13 and 37:14.
biblical_def: Irijah is the officer who laid hands on the prophet. Jeremiah was leaving Jerusalem for Benjamin during a lull in the siege, “And when he was in the gate of Benjamin, a captain of the ward was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah; and he took Jeremiah the prophet, saying, Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans” (Jeremiah 37:13). The prophet denied it flatly: “Then said Jeremiah, It is false; I fall not away to the Chaldeans. But he hearkened not to him: so Irijah took Jeremiah, and brought him to the princes” (Jeremiah 37:14). What followed was a beating and a dungeon: “Wherefore the princes were wroth with Jeremiah, and smote him, and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe: for they had made that the prison” (Jeremiah 37:15). The charge was treason, and it was plausible, because Jeremiah had been telling Jerusalem for years that the city would fall and that submission to Babylon was the LORD's word. The man whose name means the LORD seeth could not see that the one prophet telling Judah the truth was the only patriot left in the gate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Irijah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the LORD seeth; the captain of the ward in the gate of Benjamin who arrested Jeremiah on a charge of desertion.
webster_full: Hebrew Yir'iyyah, the LORD seeth, or whom Jehovah regards.
From ra'ah, to see, to look upon, compounded with Yah.
It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, Jeremiah 37:13 and 37:14.
He is called the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah.
He was a captain of the ward in the gate of Benjamin at Jerusalem.

And it came to pass, that when the army of the Chaldeans was broken up from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh's army,
corruption_summary: The man who tells an endangered nation the truth is read as its enemy; Jeremiah was beaten for the only counsel that would have saved lives.
corruption_paragraphs: A besieged city has no patience for a prophet who says the siege will succeed, and Irijah's accusation had the ring of common sense. The structure repeats whenever a people decide that loyalty means agreement: the one who warns is reclassified as the threat, and the warning is answered with a prison rather than a reply. Jeremiah's denial was true and was not even weighed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness to God's word may look exactly like disloyalty to men, and must be borne anyway. “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Matthew 5:11). Irijah acted within his office and was still wrong, which is the sober warning in the passage: lawful authority does not sanctify a false charge.

pos: n. (a man of God whose sons kept a chamber in the house of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Yigdalyahu, the LORD is great, or whom Jehovah makes great, from gadal, to be great or to magnify, with Yah; named once, Jeremiah 35:4.
biblical_def: Igdaliah is named once, and only as a father and a landmark: “And I brought them into the house of the LORD, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which was by the chamber of the princes, which was above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the door” (Jeremiah 35:4). The title given him — a man of God — is the standing biblical designation of a prophet, and it is attached to him in passing, as a thing everyone knew. The chamber mattered because of what happened in it. The LORD had told Jeremiah, “Go unto the house of the Rechabites, and speak unto them, and bring them into the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink” (Jeremiah 35:2). The Rechabites refused, because their father Jonadab had commanded them to drink no wine, and their obedience to a dead man's word became God's indictment of Judah's disobedience to His own. The verdict stands to this day: “Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever” (Jeremiah 35:19). Igdaliah's family chamber was the room where that sermon was preached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Igdaliah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the LORD is great; called a man of God, whose sons kept a chamber in the temple used by Jeremiah to test the Rechabites.
webster_full: Hebrew Yigdalyahu, the LORD is great, or whom Jehovah magnifies.

He is styled a man of God, the ordinary scriptural title of a prophet.
His son was Hanan, whose sons had a chamber in the house of the LORD.
scriptures: Jer 35:4

And I brought them into the house of the LORD, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which was by the chamber of the princes, which was above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the door:
Jer 35:2
Go unto the house of the Rechabites, and speak unto them, and bring them into the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink.
Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever.

The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab, that he commanded his sons not to drink wine, are performed; for unto this day they drink none, but obey their father's commandment: notwithstanding I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye hearkened not unto me.
corruption_summary: Obedience handed down from a father is treated as an inherited burden to be outgrown; in Jeremiah 35 it is the standard by which a nation is judged.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct treats the commandments of a forefather as a constraint on authenticity: each generation must decide afresh, and continuity with the fathers is suspected of being mere conditioning. Jeremiah 35 sets a household against a kingdom on exactly this point. The Rechabites kept a command given generations earlier by a man long dead, and God commended them, not because the rule itself was moral law, but because they had kept faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of a godly inheritance. “The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab, that he commanded his sons not to drink wine, are performed; for unto this day they drink none, but obey their father's commandment: notwithstanding I have spoken unto you” (Jeremiah 35:14). The room where it was proved belonged to the sons of a man of God, and the LORD saw to it that his name was written down with theirs.

pos: n. (a son of Shaphan who carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon; also a priest in Ezra's day)
etymology: Hebrew El'asah, God hath made, from El, God, and asah, to do or make; named at Jeremiah 29:3 and Ezra 10:22.
biblical_def: Two men bear the name, and the better known of them carried one of the most consequential letters in the Old Testament. Zedekiah sent an embassy to Nebuchadnezzar, and Jeremiah used it as his post: the prophecy went “By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying” (Jeremiah 29:3). What he carried was the letter to the captives, and it overturned everything the exiles were being told by the prophets among them: build houses, plant gardens, take wives, seek the peace of the city, for the captivity would be seventy years and no sooner. The LORD addressed it “unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon” (Jeremiah 29:4) — caused, not merely permitted. The other Elasah is a priest of the sons of Pashur who had taken a strange wife and put her away (Ezra 10:22). The name means God hath made, and one of the two men spent a journey carrying the proof that God had made even the exile.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Elasah, a Hebrew proper name signifying God hath made; a son of Shaphan who bore Jeremiah's letter to the captives in Babylon, and a priest in Ezra's day.
webster_full: Hebrew El'asah, God hath made or God hath done.
From El, God, compounded with asah, to do, make or work.
It occurs twice in this spelling in the Authorized Version, Jeremiah 29:3 and Ezra 10:22.
The first was a son of Shaphan, sent by Zedekiah on embassy to Babylon.
The second was of the sons of Pashur, who put away a strange wife.
scriptures: Jer 29:3
By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying,
Jer 29:4
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon;
And of the sons of Pashur; Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethaneel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
corruption_summary: Exile is read as the failure of God's promise; Jeremiah's letter says God caused it, set its term, and commanded His people to live faithfully inside it.
corruption_paragraphs: A disaster on this scale invites one of two errors: deny it will last, or conclude that God has abandoned the covenant. The prophets in Babylon took the first, promising a quick return, and Jeremiah's letter demolished them. It also refused the second. The captivity is from God's own hand, it has a fixed term, and in the meantime the captives are to build, plant, marry and pray — “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it” (Jeremiah 29:7).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the absolute sovereignty of God over the worst that befalls His people, and the ordinary obedience He requires of them under it. Nothing in the letter is sentimental and nothing in it despairs. A man named God hath made carried it four hundred miles to people who needed to hear exactly that.

pos: n. (an ancestor of the men of Judah who dwelt at Jerusalem; also the father of Zaccur who built the wall)
etymology: Hebrew Imri, eloquent, or my word, from amar, to say or speak; named at 1 Chronicles 9:4 and Nehemiah 3:2.
biblical_def: Imri is named twice, in two books written about the same resettlement. The first notice places him in the descent of the men of Judah who came back to live in Jerusalem: “Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah” (1 Chronicles 9:4). The second names his son at work on the wall: “And next unto him builded the men of Jericho. And next to them builded Zaccur the son of Imri” (Nehemiah 3:2). Nehemiah 3 is a wall built in named sections — priests, goldsmiths, apothecaries, rulers of districts, men of Jericho and Tekoa, each stretch credited to the household that raised it. The chapter opens with the high priest himself laying hands to it: “Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests, and they builded the sheep gate” (Nehemiah 3:1). Imri's name means eloquent, and his son is remembered for stones rather than speech, which is the chapter's whole temper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Imri, a Hebrew proper name signifying eloquent, or my word; an ancestor in the line of Pharez, and the father of Zaccur who repaired the wall of Jerusalem.

Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
corruption_summary: Public work is credited to leaders and movements; Nehemiah 3 credits it household by household, by name, section by section.
corruption_paragraphs: A wall rebuilt in fifty-two days is the kind of achievement later told as one man's story. Nehemiah refused to tell it that way. His third chapter is a list of builders — who built what, next to whom — and it includes the goldsmiths, the apothecaries, the daughters of Shallum, and Zaccur the son of Imri. The governor's name appears nowhere in the construction credits.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's work is done by named people doing adjacent portions. “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6). The joining is the miracle, and the list is how we know who did the joining.

pos: n. (a Benjamite ancestor at Jerusalem; also the father of Ahab the false prophet in Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Qolayah, voice of the LORD, from qol, a voice or sound, with Yah; named at Nehemiah 11:7 and Jeremiah 29:21.
biblical_def: Two men carry this name, and the second is remembered only for his son. The first is a Benjamite in the resettlement of Jerusalem: “And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah” (Nehemiah 11:7). The second stands in Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, in the sentence passed on two men who were prophesying lies in the LORD's name among the captives: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes” (Jeremiah 29:21). Their end became a byword: “And of them shall be taken up a curse by all the captivity of Judah which are in Babylon, saying, The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire” (Jeremiah 29:22). A name meaning the voice of the LORD was borne by the father of a man who counterfeited it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Kolaiah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the voice of the LORD; a Benjamite ancestor, and the father of Ahab the false prophet slain in Babylon.
webster_full: Hebrew Qolayah, the voice of the LORD.

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes;
And of them shall be taken up a curse by all the captivity of Judah which are in Babylon, saying, The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire;

Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: False prophecy is treated as a difference of opinion about the future; Scripture treats it as speaking lies in the name of God, and judges it accordingly.
corruption_paragraphs: Men who claim divine authority for their own words are still with us, and the modern response is to call it unhelpful rather than wicked. Jeremiah 29 names the crime precisely: they prophesy a lie unto you in my name. The LORD adds a second charge, that they “have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them” (Jeremiah 29:23). Doctrinal fraud and moral fraud travelled together, as they usually do.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the name of God is not available for private use. The punishment was public and the proverb that came of it was public, because the captives needed a standing reminder that a comforting word is not thereby a true one. The closed canon is the church's protection against the sons of Kolaiah.

pos: n. (a Netophathite whose son Seraiah came to Gedaliah at Mizpah)
etymology: Hebrew Tanchumeth, consolation, from nacham, to comfort or console; named twice, 2 Kings 25:23 and Jeremiah 40:8.
biblical_def: Tanhumeth is named in both accounts of the gathering at Mizpah after Jerusalem fell. “And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men” (2 Kings 25:23); Jeremiah gives the same roll (Jeremiah 40:8). These were the remnant of Judah's field officers, coming in to a governor appointed by the conqueror. Gedaliah's counsel to them was plain: “Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon” (2 Kings 25:24). It was good counsel and it was Jeremiah's own, and within two months Ishmael the son of Nethaniah murdered Gedaliah and the little commonwealth collapsed. The name Tanhumeth means consolation, and his son is listed among the last men who might have had some, and did not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Tanhumeth, a Hebrew proper name signifying consolation; a Netophathite whose son Seraiah came in to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem.
webster_full: Hebrew Tanchumeth, consolation or comfort.

It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, 2 Kings 25:23 and Jeremiah 40:8.
He is called the Netophathite, of the town of Netophah near Bethlehem.
His son Seraiah was a captain of the forces who came to Gedaliah.
scriptures: And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men.
Jer 40:8

Then they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, and the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men.
And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you.
Jer 40:9

And Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan sware unto them and to their men, saying, Fear not to serve the Chaldeans: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.
corruption_summary: Submission to a judgment God has declared is read as cowardice; Gedaliah's counsel was Jeremiah's counsel, and the men who rejected it destroyed what was left.
corruption_paragraphs: There is always a party that calls surrender treason. After the city fell, the captains who came in to Mizpah faced a hard choice between a patriotism that had already failed and a submission the prophet had commanded for forty years. Those who took Gedaliah's word planted and gathered wine and summer fruits in abundance. Those who did not murdered him and fled to Egypt, which Jeremiah had expressly forbidden.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that when God has pronounced a chastisement, the godly course is to bear it and work within it, not to fight the hand that holds the rod. “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lamentations 3:26). The consolation in Tanhumeth's name was available at Mizpah, and it was refused.

pos: n. (the designation of two men, Jehdeiah under David and Jadon under Nehemiah, from an unlocated Meronoth)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Meronothi, the Meronothite, a gentilic from the place-name Meronoth, whose site is not identified; named twice, 1 Chronicles 27:30 and Nehemiah 3:7.
biblical_def: Meronothite is a gentilic without a town. Scripture never describes Meronoth, never gives its borders, and never names it apart from the two men called by it, yet it supplies their whole public identity. The first is one of David's estate officers: “Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite” (1 Chronicles 27:30), in a chapter that ends, “All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's” (1 Chronicles 27:31). The second worked on the wall: “And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river” (Nehemiah 3:7). Both men are placed beside Gibeon and Mizpah, which suggests Meronoth lay in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. The word is a reminder that Scripture records more than it explains: a real place, real men from it, and no further information granted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Meronothite, the gentilic of Meronoth, a place not elsewhere described; applied to Jehdeiah, an officer of David, and to Jadon, a builder of the wall under Nehemiah.
webster_full: Hebrew ha-Meronothi, the Meronothite, an inhabitant of Meronoth.
The town itself is nowhere described in Scripture.
It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, 1 Chronicles 27:30 and Nehemiah 3:7.
Jehdeiah the Meronothite was over the asses of king David.
Jadon the Meronothite repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem.
scriptures: Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite:
Neh 3:7
And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river.
And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's.
Neh 3:8
Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall.
corruption_summary: Scripture's silences are read as gaps to be filled by conjecture; the honest reading is that God gave what He meant to give and no more.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the text withholds information, the temptation is to supply it — to locate Meronoth with confidence on no evidence, or to treat the obscurity as a sign that the record is unreliable. Neither is warranted. Two men are named by a town the Holy Ghost did not describe, and both are named doing real and datable work, centuries apart, in the same region.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Scripture, which includes the sufficiency of what it leaves out. “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever” (Deuteronomy 29:29). We may say Jadon repaired the wall; we may not say where he was born.

pos: n. (a descendant of Saul through Jonathan, in the Benjamite register of Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Yeho'addah, the LORD hath adorned, or whom Jehovah has decked, from adah, to pass on, and thence to deck or adorn, with the prefixed divine name; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:36.
biblical_def: Jehoadah stands in the long Benjamite register that carries Saul's house forward after the monarchy had passed to David: “And Ahaz begat Jehoadah; and Jehoadah begat Alemeth, and Azmaveth, and Zimri; and Zimri begat Moza” (1 Chronicles 8:36). The chapter before it has set the frame — “And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal” (1 Chronicles 8:33) — and the line then runs down through Merib-baal, the crippled son of Jonathan, generation by generation, long past the point where any of these men could have claimed a throne. The Chronicler keeps writing it anyway. Saul's dynasty was rejected, his sons died at Gilboa, and his great-grandson ate at David's table as a lame man; yet the house continued, named and numbered, and is counted among “the chief men” of Benjamin who dwelt at Jerusalem. A rejected line is not an erased line.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Jehoadah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the LORD hath adorned; a descendant of Saul through Jonathan, named once in 1 Chronicles 8:36.
webster_full: Hebrew Yeho'addah, the LORD hath adorned or decked.
From adah, to pass on, and thence to deck or ornament, with the divine name prefixed.
It occurs once in the Authorized Version, 1 Chronicles 8:36.
He is reckoned in the Benjamite descent of Saul through Jonathan.
His sons are given as Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri.
scriptures: And Ahaz begat Jehoadah; and Jehoadah begat Alemeth, and Azmaveth, and Zimri; and Zimri begat Moza,
And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
And the son of Jonathan was Meribbaal; and Meribbaal begat Micah.
These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: A failed house is expected to vanish from the record; the Chronicler writes Saul's descendants out to the exile, because God's dealings with a family do not end at its disgrace.
corruption_paragraphs: History written by winners omits the losing dynasty. 1 Chronicles 8 does the opposite: having given David the crown, it spends the chapter on Benjamin and on the house of Kish, tracing Saul's line through Jonathan down many generations. The men in it held no office and made no claim. They are written because they existed and because they were Israel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's covenant faithfulness reaches past the judgment He has pronounced on a house. Jonathan's descendants survived because David kept an oath to a dead friend. “And thou shalt not only while yet I live shew me the kindness of the LORD, that I die not” (1 Samuel 20:14). Jehoadah is in the Bible because a promise was kept.
